title: SQL Injection: Detection and Mitigation
summary: Recognising SQL injection attempts in logs and remediating the underlying flaw.
content:
# SQL Injection: Detection and Mitigation

## What it is
SQL injection occurs when untrusted input is concatenated into a SQL statement, letting an
attacker change the structure of the query rather than only its data. Consequences run from
authentication bypass and unauthorised data reads through to arbitrary file access and remote
code execution, depending on the database and its privileges.

## What it looks like in logs
Web and WAF logs show SQL metacharacters and keywords in parameters: single quotes, double
dashes, block comment markers, UNION SELECT, OR 1=1, SLEEP(, pg_sleep(, WAITFOR DELAY,
information_schema, xp_cmdshell. Blind and time-based injection shows as repeated
near-identical requests whose response times differ systematically. Error-based injection
produces bursts of HTTP 500s with database error text in the response body.

A long run of requests to one endpoint varying a single parameter, with alternating success
and error responses, is the signature of automated tooling such as sqlmap.

## Triage
Identify the endpoint and parameter under attack, then determine whether any attempt
succeeded: look for anomalous response sizes, unexpected 200s among the errors, and database
logs showing statements the application would never legitimately issue. Check whether the
database account used by the application is over-privileged - a successful injection against
a read-only account is a very different incident from one against a database owner.

## Containment
Block the source at the WAF and add a rule for the observed pattern. Take the vulnerable
endpoint out of service if exploitation succeeded. Preserve database audit logs before they
roll. Assume any data readable by the application account was exposed, and scope the
notification obligations accordingly.

## Remediation
Use parameterised queries or prepared statements everywhere; never build SQL by string
concatenation. Validate and canonicalise input by allowlist. Apply least privilege to the
application database account. Disable verbose database errors in production responses. Add
a regression test that submits the exploit payload and asserts it is handled as data.
